name: Maya Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for talking with me, Maya. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential. Could you start by telling me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I spray shotcrete underground at a zinc mine, which is concrete you blast onto the rock walls so they don't fall in on anyone. I'm in the cage going down by half six, then I drive the sprayer rig to wherever the drill crew finished blasting. Before this I was a school cook for thirty years, so I'm the oldest trainee they've ever had, and the shift boss, Priya, still checks my nozzle work twice.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Why the switch to mining at your age?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Money, plainly. My pension from the school kitchen is small, and the mine pays nearly double, so I thought five or six good years would make a real difference. My partner Jonas works for the council parks team, and between us we can see the finish line now.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the crew, and I like seeing a fresh wall sprayed smooth and knowing I made that heading safe. The hard part is my knees on the ladders, and feeling slow. The young ones read the rock just by looking at it, and I'm still asking what I'm looking at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, there you go, all that worry for a better spell-checker. I'd probably post something cheeky in the family group chat. At work I'd say the real problem was always the ventilation and the pay, not the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my plan works. Five or six years on the sprayer, pension topped up, then out at sixty-three or sixty-four. I'd be pleased, really, though part of me is curious what we missed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Exactly what I'm doing now. I'd keep going with my training and try to get signed off on the loader too. I'd keep using the AI thing on my phone now and then, like when I wrote my letter to the pension fund last month, because it's handy for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and a bit smug, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the letter to the pension fund. How did that go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I asked the phone to help me write it because I always sound either rude or grovelling in letters. It came out clear and polite, and I got an answer in two weeks. My daughter showed me how, and now I use it maybe once a month for things like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: As the new health and safety rep, would anything change in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. Maybe the gas readings come through a bit smarter. But I'd still be the one standing at the face asking if the bolts are in before anyone goes under fresh ground, and no clever app changes that.

S0.say: I'd say all that worry was for a better spell-checker, and the real problems were always ventilation and pay. She'd post something cheeky in the family group chat.
S0.think: Privately she'd be pleased, because her plan of five or six well-paid years topping up a small pension would still work. She'd retire at sixty-three or sixty-four, though part of her would be curious what they missed.
S0.do: Keeps training on the sprayer and works towards being signed off on the loader. Keeps using AI on her phone now and then for jobs like letters to the pension fund.
S0.quote: I'd still be the one standing at the face asking if the bolts are in before anyone goes under fresh ground, and no clever app changes that.
S0.fieldNote: Maya came into mining late and on purpose, with a clear money plan. She already uses AI casually and sees it as a small helper, not a threat. Her pride in being the safety rep came through strongly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say change is fine as long as the people doing the work get a say in it, and the savings go to wages and safety, not just the shareholders. I'd bring it up at the union meeting as a safety question first, because that's where they have to listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think underground changes slower than people think. The ground's different every day and the robots I've seen on videos don't cope with wet, broken rock. But I'm the newest operator, so if they need fewer of us, they won't keep the fifty-eight-year-old trainee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the company straight away what training is on offer for the new kit and put my name down once a few others had been through it, so I know it's real. I'd move another couple of hundred a month into savings. And I'd have a talk with Jonas about whether we could both retire at sixty-three if my mine years got cut short.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like a noise in the car you can't quite place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait for others to go through the training first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've watched companies announce shiny programmes that vanish in six months. When the canteen got its new ordering system, I waited until the cooks on the other site said it worked. Then I learned it in a week and ended up teaching the head cook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at the mine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The young lads on the drill rigs with babies at home. I've got my kitchen skills to fall back on and a grown-up family. They've only ever known this, and some of them have huge loans on their utes.

S1.say: I'd say change is fine if workers get a say and the savings go to wages and safety, not just shareholders. She'd raise it at the union meeting as a safety question first.
S1.think: She thinks underground work will change more slowly than people expect, because the rock is different every day. Still, as the newest operator, she knows she'd be an easy one to let go.
S1.do: Signs up for training on the new equipment once a few others have proved it's real. Moves a couple of hundred more a month into savings and talks with Jonas about both retiring at sixty-three.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like a noise in the car she can't place.
S1.quote: I waited until the cooks on the other site said it worked. Then I learned it in a week and ended up teaching the head cook.
S1.fieldNote: Her "wait until it's proven, then learn it fast" approach shows up clearly with a real example. She frames her union concerns through safety, which is clever and practical. She worries more for young drillers with debts than for herself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for the unions and the government to step in hard, before it's all over. Tax the machines, slow it down, protect people. I'd be at the rally with a sign, and I'd tell everyone at work to join if they haven't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be scared. Two years means I'd lose the mine job before I'd built up the extra pension I came for. And the fallback I always had, going back to a kitchen, is gone too if robots can cook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop all the extras straight away, the holiday to see my sister and the new kitchen bench we'd saved for. I'd ask the union about a redundancy package and whether I could get my pension early at sixty. I'd look for anything people still want a human for, maybe aged care, because I've a feeling families will still want a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like the cage dropping too fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much do you have saved, and how long would it last?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About five months if we keep living as we do, maybe eight if we cut right back. Jonas's council job would carry us a bit, but councils will be cutting too. The kitchen bench money would go straight into the pot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said underground changes slowly. Does that hold here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not if the robots really can do anything. I said that about the slow change, and I believe it there. In this one I'm just hoping, and hope's not a plan.

S2.say: I'd say the unions and government need to step in hard now: tax the machines, slow it down and protect people. She'd go to the rally and urge everyone at work to join the union.
S2.think: She'd be scared that she'd lose the mine job before building the extra pension she came for. Her old fallback, going back to a kitchen, would vanish too if robots can cook.
S2.do: Cancels the trip to see her sister and the new kitchen bench, putting the money into savings. Asks the union about a redundancy package and drawing her pension at sixty, and looks into aged care work.
S2.feel: Alarmed, like the cage dropping too fast.
S2.quote: The fallback I always had, going back to a kitchen, is gone too if robots can cook.
S2.fieldNote: The loss of her backup plan is what turns her from uneasy to alarmed. She caught her own earlier argument about slow change and dropped it honestly. Her instinct to look at aged care shows her belief that some work will stay human.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's use them: proper retraining, a fund paid for by the companies, and older workers looked after. I'd say it at union meetings and I'd write to our MP, probably with a bit of help from the phone to get the words right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be sixty-three by 2031, which was roughly my plan anyway. So the deadline and my retirement more or less meet in the middle. If I can stay on for most of it, I'll get most of what I came to the mine for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put the kitchen bench money and every bit of overtime into savings for three or four years, aiming to have a year's worth put away. I'd do the training on the new automated kit once it's proven on other shifts, so I'm useful during the changeover. And I'd volunteer at the aged care home on weekends, just to see if it's something I could do after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a way I can work with. I like having a deadline to plan against.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the aged care volunteering tell you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether I'm any good at it, mostly. Cooking for six hundred kids was one thing; sitting with someone who's frightened is another. My mum was in a home at the end, and the staff who were good with her had something you can't teach in a course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the extra three years change compared with the fast one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everything about how it feels. Two years is a door slamming. Five years is a door closing slowly, and you can get your coat and say goodbye to people on the way out.

S3.say: I'd say five years should be used for proper retraining, a company-funded fund and protection for older workers. She'd raise it at union meetings and write to her MP with some help from AI.
S3.think: She'd turn sixty-three in 2031, close to her planned retirement, so the deadline and her plans roughly line up. If she can stay for most of it, she'll get most of what she came for.
S3.do: Puts overtime and the kitchen bench money into savings for three or four years, aiming for a year's cushion. Trains on the new automated equipment once it's proven and volunteers at an aged care home on weekends.
S3.feel: Anxious but able to work with it, since a deadline gives her something to plan against.
S3.quote: Two years is a door slamming. Five years is a door closing slowly, and you can get your coat and say goodbye to people on the way out.
S3.fieldNote: For Maya, time is the whole difference: five years nearly matches her retirement plan. She combines collective action with practical personal steps, like testing aged care work before needing it. The memory of her mum's carers made her thinking about human work very concrete.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is time to do it right, and if we don't, that's a choice the government made. I'd keep pushing the union on it, because the young ones will be the ones it hits. Online, I'd share the sensible articles and ignore the doom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's fine. I'll be retired by then, sixty-three if things go to plan, and I'll have had my good years at the mine. I'd worry for my two daughters, one's a nurse and one works in an office, and I'd guess the office one is more exposed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with my plan, get signed off on the loader, and retire at sixty-three. I'd tell my daughter in the office to start looking at what she could do with her hands or with people, maybe nursing like her sister. And I'd still keep the union going on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really, with a little worry for the girls tucked in behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your daughter in the office?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, love, I changed jobs at fifty-four, you can do it at thirty-two. I'd probably say it over Sunday lunch so she can't storm off. She'd tell me I don't understand her job, and she'd be right, but I understand starting over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change anything about money in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. Maybe keep the kitchen bench plan, which Jonas will be pleased about. We'd keep saving as we are, and I wouldn't touch the pension early.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is time to do it properly, and failing would be the government's choice. She'd keep pushing the union for the young ones and share sensible articles online.
S4.think: She expects to be retired by then and to have had her good mine years. Her worry is her daughters, especially the one in an office job.
S4.do: Carries on with her plan, gets signed off on the loader and retires at sixty-three. Urges her office-worker daughter to look at hands-on or people work and keeps pushing the union.
S4.feel: Calm, with a small worry for her daughters.
S4.quote: I'd say, love, I changed jobs at fifty-four, you can do it at thirty-two.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade of warning, Maya's own plan is safe and she relaxes. She offers her own late career change as proof to her daughter. Her union commitment stays steady even when she's not at risk herself.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it takes away both the mine and the kitchen at once. What would help is the company and the government agreeing a bridge to the pension for people over fifty-five, and real training places in care work, not just a website.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how it feels being a woman my age down there. The men have been kind, mostly, but I had to prove I wasn't a tourist. I'd hate for all that effort to end with a robot getting the respect I spent three years earning.

headlineQuote: I'd hate for all that effort to end with a robot getting the respect I spent three years earning.
portrait: Maya Larsen is a fifty-eight-year-old former school cook who sprays shotcrete underground at a zinc mine, a job she took to top up a small pension before retiring at sixty-three. She's a union member and new safety rep who uses AI now and then but waits for new things to prove themselves. She's calm if AI fizzles, uneasy with steady change, and alarmed by AGI in two years because it would take away both the mine and her old kitchen fallback. With five years she plans and feels in control, and with ten she's calm for herself and worried for her office-worker daughter.
biggestWorry: AGI in two years worries her most, because it would remove both the mine job and her fallback of kitchen work at the same time.
whatWouldHelp: A company and government bridge to the pension for workers over fifty-five, plus real training places in care work.
